title: Why is Korea split in two?
subtitle: The 38th parallel
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In August 1945, two American officers drew a line on a map: Korea, united for centuries, was cut in two. Eighty years later, the "temporary" border is still there.
author: ivana-toskovic

hero.hook: A border drawn in one night by two American officers, on a National Geographic map, and never erased since.

blocks.text: Korea was one country for a very long time. The [[Joseon dynasty]], the last to rule the peninsula, governed until **1910**. That year, Japan annexed Korea. Its rule, highly authoritarian, lasted nearly four decades. Generations of young Koreans grew up with a patriotism fed by the occupation: their goal was independence, never division.

In **1945**, Japan was defeated. The atomic bombs dropped on its territory ended World War II and freed Korea. But freedom lasted only a few days. Almost at once, the United States and the Soviet Union split the country into two halves. How could a nation united for so long be cut in two?

sections.title: A border drawn in one night on a map

blocks.text: Nothing required this partition. Koreans shared the same origin, the same language, the same religion, and their borders had defined their nation-state for a very long time. Yet the division was done in a rush. Two American colonels were given the job of splitting the country between American and Soviet control. They drew their line in one night, on a National Geographic map.

blocks.caption: The peninsula divided at the 38th parallel in 1945: Soviet zone in the north, American zone in the south.

blocks.text: Their goal was simple: cut the country through the middle, keeping the capital, Seoul, on the American side. The [[38th parallel]] became the temporary border between a North Korea controlled by the Soviets and a South Korea under American authority. Nobody consulted the Korean people. Nor even the United Kingdom or China, which were supposed to take part in the trusteeship planned for the country.

The Moscow Agreement provided for an independent Korea, guided by a Joint Commission that met in 1946: American and Soviet representatives, Korean political parties, China and the United Kingdom. The stated goal was a democratic state. But Koreans feared that the occupation had merely changed its form.

Soon afterward, the [[Cold War]] froze the partition. The United States bet on an anti-colonial, anti-communist South: in **1948**, the [[Republic of Korea]] was born, shaped by the American military and bureaucracy. In the North, the Soviets backed a communist regime that became, the same year, the [[Democratic People's Republic of Korea]]. Korea was officially divided into two separate nations.

blocks.caption: The proclamation of the Republic of Korea in Seoul, 15 August 1948.

blocks.text: The two halves went opposite ways. South Korea became a democratic state with a thriving economy and technology, open to the world and firmly allied with the United States, backed by a professional military. North Korea became an authoritarian dictatorship, isolated both internationally and economically. Military service there is compulsory for all men, for up to **10 years**, and the regime keeps advancing its nuclear capabilities.

sections.title: The Korean War and the demilitarized zone

blocks.text: Korea's division followed the growing tensions between Americans and Soviets across the world. It became more ideological, more complex, and set the stage for the clashes to come. On **25 June 1950**, North Korea invaded the South to reunify the country under the communist regime. The invasion was backed by both the Soviets and the Chinese: the [[Korean War]] had begun.

blocks.caption: A column of Korean refugees fleeing south during the winter of 1950-1951.

blocks.text: The fighting stopped in **1953**. A [[demilitarized zone]] was established along the 38th parallel: a strip of land that no army may enter. But no peace treaty was signed. The country officially remains at war, with countless casualties and deep resentment on both sides.

sections.title: How a small country hardened the Cold War

blocks.text: The Korean War exposed the threat of Soviet expansionism to the whole world. NATO, the Western military alliance, and the entire American [[military-industrial complex]] increased their budgets. Militarization became concrete: precise commitments were made to defend allies against possible communist attacks.

Each move led to the next. Distrust between China and the United States grew. Washington now feared the Sino-Soviet alliance and saw any communist takeover, anywhere, as a direct threat to its national interests. Korea is a textbook case: a small country can directly shape the whole of international relations. Without it, the Cold War might have been less widespread and less severe.

events.title: Japanese annexation
events.detail: Japan ends the Joseon dynasty and occupies Korea for nearly forty years.

events.title: The 38th parallel
events.detail: Two American colonels split the liberated peninsula into American and Soviet zones.

events.title: Two states
events.detail: The Republic of Korea in the South, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in the North.

events.title: War begins
events.detail: The North invades the South with the backing of Moscow and Beijing.

events.title: Demilitarized zone
events.detail: The fighting stops, but no peace is signed.

blocks.text: Cut in two in 1945 by a hastily drawn line, frozen by the Cold War in 1948 and then by the war of 1950-1953, Korea remains divided by a border that nobody meant to be permanent.
